title: Hazards, perils, losses and valuation
summary: Follow Tony's Pizza in Detroit: insurable interest, underwriting, hazards vs perils, construction classes, direct vs indirect loss and valuing a loss.
objectives: Explain insurable interest, underwriting and the loss ratio
Tell physical, moral and morale hazards apart, and a hazard from a peril
Contrast open vs named perils, blanket vs specific, direct vs indirect loss
Value a loss: replacement cost, ACV, functional, stated amount, agreed value

scenes.title: Tony's big move
scenes.subtitle: How an insurer sizes up Tony's pizza shop, and how it puts a dollar value on a loss

beats.text: Meet Tony, who just moved his pizza shop into a bigger Detroit building. His week covers Property and Casualty Basics: 20% of your exam, about 30 questions.
beats.say: Meet Tony, who just moved his pizza shop into a bigger Detroit building. His week covers Property and Casualty Basics: twenty percent of your exam, about thirty questions.

beats.text: New shop, new oven. What could possibly go wrong?
beats.say: New shop, new oven. What could possibly go wrong?

scenes.title: Why Tony can insure his building
scenes.src: IRMI glossary: insurable interest; ISO CP 00 10 10 12, E.4.d; ISO HO 00 03 05 11, Sec. I Cond. A; question core-021
scenes.plain: A real stake in what's insured, financial or legal. It usually comes from property rights like ownership, a contract, or potential legal liability.
scenes.example: Tony owns his new building and the ovens inside, so he has an insurable interest in both.
scenes.exam: Property: it must exist at the time of the loss, and you're paid no more than your interest. Liability: it comes from potential legal liability.

beats.text: Tony owns his building and ovens, so he has an insurable interest in them: a financial or legal relationship to what's insured.
beats.say: Tony owns his building and ovens, so he has an insurable interest in them: a financial or legal relationship to what's insured.

beats.text: For property insurance, it must exist at the time of the loss. For liability, it comes from your potential legal liability.
beats.say: For property insurance, it must exist at the time of the loss. For liability, it comes from your potential legal liability.

scenes.title: Tony's call: the old shop burns
scenes.src: ISO CP 00 10 10 12, E.4.d; ISO HO 00 03 05 11, Sec. I Cond. A and Cond. E (Assignment); IRMI: insurable interest; question core-021

draw.text: March: Tony sold this empty shop to a baker
Uh oh. I never canceled that policy.

beats.text: In March, Tony sold his empty old shop to a baker, but forgot to cancel its insurance. In May, it burns. What does Tony do?
beats.say: In March, Tony sold his empty old shop to a baker, but forgot to cancel its insurance. In May, it burns. What does Tony do?

options.label: Claim it. I still pay the premium!
options.fail: Paying the premium isn't enough. For property insurance, insurable interest must exist at the time of the loss, and Tony sold the shop in March.

beats.text: Tony files. The insurer pays nothing: when it burned, the shop wasn't his.
beats.say: Tony files. The insurer pays nothing: when it burned, the shop wasn't his.

beats.text: But I paid!
beats.say: But I paid!

draw.text: Not his shop when it burned

options.label: Claim it. I owned it when the policy began!
options.fail: Owning it when the policy began isn't enough. Property insurance pays no more than your interest at the time of the loss.

beats.text: Owning it then doesn't count. He's paid no more than his interest when it burned: zero.
beats.say: Owning it then doesn't count. He's paid no more than his interest when it burned: zero.

draw.text: In May, the baker owned it

options.label: Skip it. The baker owned it when it burned
options.win: Interest must exist at the time of loss. In May, the shop was the baker's, and Tony's policy can't pass to her without the insurer's written consent.

beats.text: Right. When it burned, the shop was the baker's. Tony had no interest left.
beats.say: Right. When it burned, the shop was the baker's. Tony had no interest left.

draw.text: The owner at the time of loss
Not my shop. Not my claim.

reveal.text: For property, insurable interest must exist at the time of the loss.
reveal.say: For property, insurable interest must exist at the time of the loss.

scenes.title: The underwriter sizes up Tony
scenes.src: IRMI glossary: underwriting; loss ratio; expense ratio; combined ratio; questions core-bas-02, core-022

goal.text: Say the insurer's book has $100,000 of earned premium. Find the incurred losses that make a 50% loss ratio.

beats.text: Dana sends Tony's application to the insurance company. An underwriter decides: accept the risk? How much insurance? At what rate?
beats.say: Dana sends Tony's application to the insurance company. An underwriter decides: accept the risk? How much insurance? At what rate?

beats.text: Paying claims? That's claims handling, not underwriting.
beats.say: Paying claims? That's claims handling, not underwriting.

beats.text: Underwriters also watch the loss ratio across their book of business: incurred losses divided by earned premium. Your turn.
beats.say: Underwriters also watch the loss ratio across their book of business: incurred losses divided by earned premium. Your turn.

reveal.say: Fifty thousand dollars of losses: a fifty percent loss ratio.

reveal.text: Add the expense ratio, underwriting expenses divided by premium, to get the combined ratio. Under 100% means an underwriting profit.
reveal.say: Add the expense ratio, underwriting expenses divided by premium, to get the combined ratio. Under one hundred percent means an underwriting profit.

scenes.title: Hazards: Property, Person, Meh
scenes.src: IRMI glossary: hazard; physical, moral, morale hazard; peril; question core-bas-03; cp_personal-01; adapted from hook mn_core-10

draw.text: A fire would pay my debts...
Character or circumstances: dishonesty, a motive to profit from a loss
Fire, tornado: a PERIL, the cause of loss, not a hazard

beats.text: Next, the underwriter hunts for hazards: conditions that raise the chance of loss. Think Property, Person, Meh.
beats.say: Next, the underwriter hunts for hazards: conditions that raise the chance of loss. Think Property, Person, Meh.

beats.text: Physical hazard, the Property: a tangible condition, like oily rags piled next to a furnace.
beats.say: Physical hazard, the Property: a tangible condition, like oily rags piled next to a furnace.

beats.text: Moral hazard, the Person: dishonesty, like a fraud record, or a motive to profit from a loss, like a money-losing business.
beats.say: Moral hazard, the Person: dishonesty, like a fraud record, or a motive to profit from a loss, like a money-losing business.

beats.text: Morale hazard, Meh: a tenant stops locking her door because insurance will pay. An attitude, not dishonesty.
beats.say: Morale hazard, Meh: a tenant stops locking her door because insurance will pay. An attitude, not dishonesty.

beats.text: And a fire or a tornado? That's the peril: the cause of loss, not a hazard.
beats.say: And a fire or a tornado? That's the peril: the cause of loss, not a hazard.

scenes.title: Your turn: which hazard?
scenes.src: IRMI glossary: physical, moral and morale hazard; cp_personal-01 drills; question core-023

cards.text: A store owner stops locking the back door: 'insurance will pay if anything is stolen.'
cards.why: Indifference to loss because insurance will pay is morale hazard: an attitude, not dishonesty.

cards.text: A home has frayed, outdated electrical wiring.
cards.why: It is a structural feature of the property that raises the chance of a fire: a physical hazard.

cards.text: An applicant has two prior convictions for insurance fraud.
cards.why: It reflects the insured's character and honesty: moral hazard.

cards.text: A driver leaves his keys in the car because insurance will pay if it's stolen.
cards.why: Carelessness because insurance will pay is morale hazard: an attitude problem, not dishonesty.

cards.text: A restaurant owner deep in debt buys a large fire policy on the failing business.
cards.why: The insured's circumstances create a motive to profit from a loss: moral hazard.

beats.text: Your turn: physical, moral or morale?
beats.say: Your turn: physical, moral or morale?

reveal.text: Physical: the property. Moral: dishonesty or a motive to profit from a loss. Morale: meh, careless because insurance will pay.
reveal.say: Physical: the property. Moral: dishonesty or a motive to profit from a loss. Morale: meh, careless because insurance will pay.

scenes.title: Tony's call: the night before the inspection
scenes.src: IRMI glossary: physical hazard; morale hazard; peril; question core-bas-03; hook mn_core-10

beats.text: The underwriter inspects tomorrow, and Tony spots oily rags piled next to the furnace. What does he do?
beats.say: The underwriter inspects tomorrow, and Tony spots oily rags piled next to the furnace. What does he do?

options.label: Toss them: they're a physical hazard
options.win: A hazard is a condition that raises the chance of loss. Getting rid of the oily rags by the furnace removes that physical hazard.

beats.text: Out they go!
beats.say: Out they go!

beats.text: Smart. Rags gone: one physical hazard fixed before the underwriter arrives.
beats.say: Smart. Rags gone: one physical hazard fixed before the underwriter arrives.

options.label: Leave them. Insurance pays for fires!
options.fail: Oily rags by a furnace are a physical hazard. Shrugging because insurance will pay is morale hazard. Moral would be dishonesty, like a fraud record.

beats.text: The underwriter writes up two hazards: the rags are physical, and Tony's shrug is morale.
beats.say: The underwriter writes up two hazards: the rags are physical, and Tony's shrug is morale.

options.label: Toss them: fire's the hazard here!
options.fail: Fire is a peril: the cause of loss. The oily rags by the furnace were the hazard: a condition that raises the chance of loss.

beats.text: Right move, wrong word. Fire is the peril, the cause of loss. The rags were the hazard.
beats.say: Right move, wrong word. Fire is the peril, the cause of loss. The rags were the hazard.

reveal.text: Rags: the hazard, raising the chance of loss. Fire: the peril, the cause of loss.
reveal.say: Rags: the hazard, raising the chance of loss. Fire: the peril, the cause of loss.

scenes.title: What's it made of? Six construction classes
scenes.src: IRMI glossary: frame, joisted masonry, noncombustible, masonry noncombustible, (modified) fire resistive construction; question core-033

draw.text: From code 1, the least fire-resistive, to code 6, the most

spots.label: Code 1: Frame
spots.text: Exterior walls of wood, brick veneer, stone veneer, wood ironclad, or stucco on wood. Brick veneer still counts as frame. The least fire-resistive.

spots.label: Code 2: Joisted masonry
spots.text: Masonry exterior walls, but a floor and roof that can burn (combustible). Tony's shop: masonry walls, wood floor and roof.

spots.label: Code 3: Noncombustible
spots.text: Exterior walls, floor and supports that won't burn: metal, asbestos, gypsum or other noncombustible materials.

spots.label: Code 4: Masonry noncombustible
spots.text: Masonry exterior walls, like code 2, but with a metal or other noncombustible floor and roof.

spots.label: Code 5: Modified fire resistive
spots.text: Masonry or fire-resistive walls, floors and roof rated at least 1 hour but less than 2 hours.

spots.label: Code 6: Fire resistive
spots.text: Walls, floors and roof rated at least 2 hours. The most fire-resistive class.

beats.text: The underwriter checks construction too. Tony's building has masonry walls and a combustible wood floor and roof: joisted masonry, code 2.
beats.say: The underwriter checks construction too. Tony's building has masonry walls and a combustible wood floor and roof: joisted masonry, code two.

beats.text: Six classes: code 1, frame, resists fire the least. Code 6, called fire resistive, resists it most. Tap each building.
beats.say: Six classes: code one, frame, resists fire the least. Code six, called fire resistive, resists it most. Tap each building.

reveal.text: Frame means wood or veneer walls. Code 5 is rated at least 1 hour but under 2. Code 6, at least 2 hours.
reveal.say: Frame means wood or veneer walls. Code five is rated at least one hour but under two. Code six, at least two hours.

scenes.title: Dana's pick: special, or open, perils
scenes.src: IRMI glossary: named perils; open perils; special perils; Heniser v Frankenmuth Mut Ins Co, 449 Mich 155 (1995); cp_personal-06
scenes.plain: Covers all causes of loss except those the policy specifically excludes. Also called special perils; formerly all risks.
scenes.example: Tony's policy lists no covered causes, only exclusions. A loss from a cause nobody thought of? Covered, unless it's excluded.
scenes.exam: Named perils covers only the perils listed. In Michigan, the insured must prove coverage; the insurer must prove an exclusion applies.

beats.text: Tony, I'd go with open perils. Everything not excluded is covered.
beats.say: Tony, I'd go with open perils. Everything not excluded is covered.

beats.text: That's special, or open, perils, formerly called all risks.
beats.say: That's special, or open, perils, formerly called all risks.

beats.text: Named perils covers only the listed perils. The tell: a list of what's covered means named; only exclusions means open.
beats.say: Named perils covers only the listed perils. The tell: a list of what's covered means named; only exclusions means open.

beats.text: In Michigan, the insured must prove coverage, and the insurer must prove an exclusion applies.
beats.say: In Michigan, the insured must prove coverage, and the insurer must prove an exclusion applies.

scenes.title: One limit or two? Specific vs blanket
scenes.src: ISO CP 03 21 10 12 (definitions); IRMI glossary: blanket limit; ISO CP 00 10 10 12, F.1.b; question core-032

draw.text: Coinsurance applies to the total value under that limit

beats.text: Specific insurance gives each item its own limit: one for the building, one for Tony's ovens and tables.
beats.say: Specific insurance gives each item its own limit: one for the building, one for Tony's ovens and tables.

beats.text: Blanket insurance puts one limit over two or more items or locations.
beats.say: Blanket insurance puts one limit over two or more items or locations.

beats.text: Coinsurance, coming later, can cut a claim payment on underinsured property. With blanket, it applies to the total value under that limit.
beats.say: Coinsurance, coming later, can cut a claim payment on underinsured property. With blanket, it applies to the total value under that limit.

scenes.title: Fire night at Tony's
scenes.src: IRMI glossary: direct loss; consequential loss; cp_personal-07; question core-031
scenes.plain: A money loss that results from direct physical damage. Also called an indirect loss.
scenes.example: Fire chars Tony's kitchen: that damage is a direct loss. The pizza sales he loses while closed for repairs are consequential.
scenes.exam: Loss of rent, business income and extra expense are consequential. Ask: is it the damage itself, or a money loss that follows?

beats.text: Then one night, fire breaks out in Tony's kitchen. The charred walls are a direct loss: direct physical damage.
beats.say: Then one night, fire breaks out in Tony's kitchen. The charred walls are a direct loss: direct physical damage.

beats.text: Tony closes for repairs and loses pizza sales: a consequential, or indirect, loss that results from the damage.
beats.say: Tony closes for repairs and loses pizza sales: a consequential, or indirect, loss that results from the damage.

scenes.title: Fire night: direct or indirect?
scenes.src: IRMI glossary: direct loss; consequential loss; cp_personal-07 drills; question core-031

items.text: Heat warps the kitchen's steel shelves
items.why: The shelves themselves are physically damaged: a direct loss.
The booths themselves are physically damaged: a direct loss.

items.text: Catering orders Tony loses while closed
items.why: Lost business income results from the damage: an indirect, or consequential, loss.

items.text: Water from the fire hoses soaks the floor
items.why: Water damage from fighting the fire is physical damage to the property: direct.

items.text: Rent lost on the upstairs apartment, now unlivable
items.why: Loss of rent results from the damage: an indirect loss.

items.text: Extra costs to run a temporary kitchen during repairs
items.why: Extra expense results from the damage: an indirect loss.

beats.text: Your turn: direct or indirect? Sort Tony's losses.
beats.say: Your turn: direct or indirect? Sort Tony's losses.

reveal.text: Damage to the property itself is direct. Lost rent, business income and extra expense are indirect.
reveal.say: Damage to the property itself is direct. Lost rent, business income and extra expense are indirect.

scenes.title: Replacement cost, ACV or functional?
scenes.src: IRMI glossary: replacement cost; actual cash value; functional replacement cost; hook mn_core-16
scenes.hook: Replacement cost buys it new. ACV blows out the birthday candles: the new price minus depreciation. Functional replacement only has to do the same job.
items: Replacement cost: like kind and quality, no deduction for depreciation
Actual cash value: often replacement cost minus depreciation
ACV can also be fair market value or the broad evidence rule
Functional replacement: does the same job equally well, need not be identical

beats.text: Take Tony's oven. Replacement cost buys it new. Actual cash value, or ACV, blows out the birthday candles: the new price minus depreciation. Functional replacement only has to do the same job.
beats.say: Take Tony's oven. Replacement cost buys it new. Actual cash value, or A C V, blows out the birthday candles: the new price minus depreciation. Functional replacement only has to do the same job.

beats.text: Replacement cost means like kind and quality, with no deduction for depreciation.
beats.say: Replacement cost means like kind and quality, with no deduction for depreciation.

beats.text: Depending on the policy and state law, ACV can also be fair market value, or the broad evidence rule, which weighs all relevant evidence of value.
beats.say: Depending on the policy and state law, A C V can also be fair market value, or the broad evidence rule, which weighs all relevant evidence of value.

scenes.q: The fire also destroyed Tony's roof. It would cost $20,000 to replace today and has depreciated 40%. Using replacement cost minus depreciation, its actual cash value is:
scenes.why: Depreciation is 40% of $20,000, or $8,000. ACV is $20,000 minus $8,000: $12,000. The $8,000 is the depreciation, not the ACV.

beats.text: The fire also destroyed Tony's roof. Your turn: what's its ACV?
beats.say: The fire also destroyed Tony's roof. Your turn: what's its A C V?

reveal.text: $12,000. 40% of $20,000 is $8,000 of depreciation, so $12,000 is left. Watch out: $8,000 is the depreciation, not the ACV.
reveal.say: Twelve thousand dollars. Forty percent of twenty thousand dollars is eight thousand dollars of depreciation, so twelve thousand dollars is left. Watch out: eight thousand dollars is the depreciation, not the A C V.

scenes.title: Tony's call: the totaled van
scenes.src: ISO CA 99 28 03 10, B.1-3, C.1 and Schedule note (2010 Stated Amount endorsement); question core-bas-12; hook mn_core-17

beats.text: Tony's van has $30,000 of stated amount coverage, common for auto physical damage, under the 2010 Stated Amount endorsement.
beats.say: Tony's van has thirty thousand dollars of stated amount coverage, common for auto physical damage, under the twenty ten stated amount endorsement.

beats.text: It's totaled in a covered collision: actual cash value $26,000, like-kind replacement $28,000. Ignore the deductible. What does Tony do?
beats.say: It's totaled in a covered collision: actual cash value twenty six thousand dollars, like-kind replacement twenty eight thousand dollars. Ignore the deductible. What does Tony do?

options.label: Demand the full $30,000 stated amount
options.fail: Stated amount pays the least of ACV, the cost to repair or replace, or the stated amount. $30,000 is a ceiling, not a guarantee.

beats.text: But the policy says $30,000!
beats.say: But the policy says thirty thousand dollars!

beats.text: Nope. That's a ceiling, not a promise.
beats.say: Nope. That's a ceiling, not a promise.

options.label: Take $26,000, the actual cash value
options.win: Under the 2010 endorsement, the insurer pays the least of ACV, repair or replacement cost, or the stated amount: here, $26,000 before any deductible.

beats.text: Right. $26,000 is the least of the three.
beats.say: Right. Twenty six thousand dollars is the least of the three.

draw.text: The least of the three, before any deductible

options.label: Demand $28,000 to replace it like-for-like
options.fail: Least of three: ACV $26,000, replacement $28,000, stated amount $30,000. The endorsement pays the least.

beats.text: Closer, but no. It pays the least of the three: $26,000.
beats.say: Closer, but no. It pays the least of the three: twenty six thousand dollars.

draw.text: The least of the three is paid

reveal.text: Stated amount pays the least of the three: here, the ACV.
reveal.say: Stated amount pays the least of the three: here, the A C V.

scenes.title: Agreed value vs. stated amount
scenes.src: ISO CP 00 10 10 12, G.1 (2012 BPP); ISO CA 99 28 03 10, B.1-3 and Schedule note (2010 Stated Amount endorsement); hook mn_core-17
scenes.hook: Agreed value sends coinsurance on vacation. Stated amount is a ceiling, not a promise: you get the LEAST of ACV, repair cost or the stated amount.
items: Stated amount (2010 auto endorsement): pays the least of three amounts
Least of: actual cash value, cost to repair or replace, or stated amount
The stated amount is a ceiling, not a guaranteed payment
Agreed value (2012 BPP option): coinsurance suspended until its expiration date

beats.text: Don't mix up these two. Agreed value sends coinsurance on vacation. Stated amount is a ceiling, not a promise.
beats.say: Don't mix up these two. Agreed value sends coinsurance on vacation. Stated amount is a ceiling, not a promise.

beats.text: Agreed value, a 2012 building and personal property form option for buildings like Tony's shop, suspends coinsurance until the agreed value expiration date.
beats.say: Agreed value, a twenty twelve building and personal property form option for buildings like Tony's shop, suspends coinsurance until the agreed value expiration date.

items: Property insurable interest must exist at the time of the loss
Hazards raise the chance of loss: Property, Person, Meh
Open perils lists only exclusions; named perils lists what's covered
ACV is often replacement cost minus depreciation
Stated amount is a ceiling; agreed value suspends coinsurance

beats.text: What a week! Once Tony sold his old shop, his insurable interest was gone. And hazards? Property, Person, Meh.
beats.say: What a week! Once Tony sold his old shop, his insurable interest was gone. And hazards? Property, Person, Meh.

beats.text: The charred kitchen was a direct loss; the lost sales, consequential. Stated amount is a ceiling; agreed value suspends coinsurance.
beats.say: The charred kitchen was a direct loss; the lost sales, consequential. Stated amount is a ceiling; agreed value suspends coinsurance.

beats.text: And no more oily rags by the furnace.
beats.say: And no more oily rags by the furnace.
